1044.title: John the Baptist's birth (24 June)
1044.hook: six months before Christmas, at midsummer, as days start shortening: he must increase, I decrease
1044.howItsDone: Churches that keep the birth of John the Baptist read Luke's account of his birth and naming, and in some places people mark the eve of the feast with bonfires.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Corpus Christi: bread carried out of the church and down the street. Your line was Christ in the streets. Now a new week.

John the Baptist's followers come to him worried. In the King James Bible: "Rabbi, he that was with thee beyond Jordan, to whom thou barest witness, behold, the same baptizeth, and all men come to him." The crowds are leaving. The man John pointed to is drawing everyone, and his river bank is getting quiet. To anyone with a following, that could sound like bad news. His followers might expect him to be hurt, or to fight back. What John says instead turns the worry inside out. And the church gives him a feast day for being born. Today, John the Baptist's birth.

John answers with a wedding. "He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled." He casts himself as the best man, whose job is not to be the groom. His joy is standing near and hearing the groom happy. Then the line: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Not through gritted teeth. As the fulfillment of his joy. Now the birth, which Luke tells with care. The angel tells Mary that her elderly cousin Elizabeth is expecting too: "this is the sixth month with her." When Mary arrives, "the babe leaped in her womb." At the birth, the neighbors expect him to be named after his father, Zacharias, who can't speak. He asks for a writing tablet and writes, "His name is John." Tradition reads Luke's sixth month this way, and the church calendar sets John's birth six months before Christmas. Some readers notice something in the sky, too. North of the equator, John's day falls just as the long days of midsummer begin to shorten, and Christmas just as the short days begin to lengthen. The light itself seems to act out his line. In some places, people light bonfires on the eve of the feast: a celebration for a man remembered for stepping aside.

Bring to mind someone near you who's doing well right now, a colleague getting noticed, a friend whose thing is working, and notice whatever comes up in you without scolding it. Then try John's posture: the friend who stands near, hears the good news, and is glad. If you pray, thank God for that person's good thing by name; if you don't, wish it bigger for them, and mean it if you can.
Bridegroom. John the Baptist's name for Jesus, calling himself only the friend who rejoices to hear the bridegroom's voice and happily steps back.
Your line: I must decrease. For John, that was joy, not loss. See you tomorrow.

1045.title: Peter and Paul (29 June)
1045.hook: the rock and the tentmaker, remembered on one day
1045.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican and Lutheran churches keep Peter and Paul together on one feast day, reading of Peter's confession and of Paul's ministry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bridegroom: the best man who was glad to step back. Your line was I must decrease.

A shared table in Antioch. Peter is eating with gentile believers. Then visitors arrive from James in Jerusalem, and Peter quietly pulls back and keeps himself apart. Paul doesn't take him aside for a private word. He writes about it later, in the King James Bible: "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed." Two leaders of the young church, disagreeing in public about who gets to sit at the table. And yet the church calendar puts them on the same day: one feast, both names. Today, Peter and Paul.
screen: `WHO GETS TO SIT AT THE TABLE?`

segments.voice: They were very different men. Peter was a fisherman from Galilee named Simon. In John's Gospel, when his brother Andrew brings him to Jesus, Jesus renames him on the spot: "thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone." Later, in Matthew: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." Paul had hunted down Jesus's followers, until a blinding light on the road to Damascus turned him around. He wrote letters, crossed seas, argued in synagogues and marketplaces, and paid his way with his hands. Acts says of him and his friends, "by their occupation they were tentmakers." The rock and the tentmaker: one walked Galilee with Jesus, the other met him on a road, after the resurrection. The word pillar comes from Paul himself, in the same letter as the row. In Jerusalem, "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars," gave him "the right hands of fellowship." A handshake across a real difference: Peter to his own people, Paul to the gentiles. So the feast doesn't pretend they always agreed. It holds them side by side, two pillars holding up one roof. Churches read Peter's place differently. Catholic teaching sees the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor and reads the rock as Peter himself; Orthodox and Protestant Christians understand the rock and Peter's role in other ways. Tradition says both men died in Rome for their faith. And a letter that carries Peter's name calls Paul "our beloved brother."

Bring to mind two people you love who are nothing alike, one loud and one quiet, maybe two who'd argue if you put them in a room. Hold each in turn, and what they give you that nobody else does. If you pray, thank God for each by name; if you don't, be grateful for them one at a time, and notice how both hold up something in your life.
Cephas. The name Jesus gave Simon, meaning a stone, later called Peter, who together with Paul the tentmaker is remembered on one feast as two pillars.
Your line: two pillars. Two different men, holding up one roof. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: Mary Magdalene (22 July)
1046.hook: the apostle to the apostles now has a full feast day
1046.howItsDone: On Mary Magdalene's day, churches that keep it read John 20's garden scene; the Catholic Church keeps it as a feast, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cephas: a fisherman and a tentmaker, once at odds, on one feast. Your line was two pillars.

Long loose hair, a jar of ointment at her elbow, eyes lifted, sometimes a skull on the table beside her. In some old paintings, that woman is Mary Magdalene, the weeping sinner. But the Gospels don't paint that picture. They never call her a prostitute. What they give her is something else entirely: a job. She's sent with a message, and the people she carries it to are the apostles themselves. That's why one of her old titles sounds like a riddle: the apostle to the apostles. Today, Mary Magdalene.

Luke introduces her among the women traveling with Jesus: "Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils." Healed, then: not a sinner in the text, someone set free. These women "ministered unto him of their substance": they paid for the mission out of their own money. John places her at the cross. And on Easter morning, in John's Gospel, she's alone at the tomb, crying, until the risen Jesus calls her by name and she knows him. Then the part that's easy to skip. He doesn't let her hold on. He gives her an errand: "go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God." And she goes. "Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the LORD, and that he had spoken these things unto her." In John, she tells them before Jesus appears to the others that evening. So where did the sinner come from? Over time, some Western preaching merged her with other women in the Gospels: the unnamed woman who weeps on Jesus's feet in Luke, and Mary of Bethany. The texts never join them. Orthodox Christians, who didn't take up that merging, honor her as equal to the apostles. The Catholic Church now keeps her day as a full feast, and uses that old title: apostle to the apostles. Different churches, one thing in common. The first words of Easter, in John, travel through her.

1047.title: The Transfiguration (6 August)
1047.hook: the mountain of light, on the same date as Hiroshima's bombing
1047.howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and some Protestant churches keep the Transfiguration on the sixth of August with readings of the mountain story, and some churches join it with prayers for peace because it shares the date of the Hiroshima bombing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene, sent from an empty tomb with news. Your line was she told them first.

Three fishermen climb behind their teacher up a high mountain, apart from everyone: Peter, James and John. Near the top, the man they've been following changes in front of them. His face shines like the sun. His clothes go white as light. Two figures from the old stories stand there talking with him. And Peter, who Mark says did not know what to say, offers to build some shelters. The church remembers that mountain on the sixth of August. In a later century, that same date became the day an atomic bomb fell on the city of Hiroshima. One date, two lights. Today, the Transfiguration.

Matthew, Mark and Luke all tell this story. Here's Matthew, in the King James Bible: Jesus "was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light." Transfigured means his form changed. Not a costume, not a trick of the sunset. Then Moses and Elijah appear, Elias in the King James, talking with him. Some readers hear the law and the prophets in those two. Peter blurts out: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias." He wants to keep the moment, to pitch a tent around it. Before he finishes, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." The disciples fall on their faces, terrified. Then Jesus touches them: "Arise, and be not afraid." They look up and "saw no man, save Jesus only." Then they walk back down, into ordinary need. Orthodox, Catholic and some Protestant calendars keep this feast. And the date now carries a second light. On the day the church reads of a light that ends with be not afraid, a light that burns made a whole city afraid. Some churches mark both together, with prayer for peace. The story doesn't make that second light smaller. It stands beside it.
screen: `HIS FACE DID SHINE AS THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Name one place where people are afraid tonight because of war; don't search for the worst image, just name the place. Then picture Jesus touching his friends on the mountain, and the words, arise, and be not afraid. If you pray, offer Jesus's words from the Sermon on the Mount, blessed are the peacemakers; if you don't, hold that place and its people quietly for the length of the sit.
The Transfiguration. The moment on the mountain when Jesus's face shone like the sun, and a voice said, hear ye him. Kept on the sixth of August.
Your line: two lights. A light on a mountain, and a light over a city. Until tomorrow.

1048.title: Mary's falling asleep (15 August)
1048.hook: Orthodox keep the Dormition, Catholics the Assumption; many Protestants simply honor Mary as a faithful disciple
1048.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep the Dormition of Mary in August, and Catholics keep the Assumption on the fifteenth; some Protestant churches keep a festival of Mary, and others simply remember her as a faithful disciple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Transfiguration: a mountain of light, and a darker date. Your line was two lights.

Here is an Orthodox icon. A woman lies on a bier, eyes closed, hands folded. The apostles crowd around her, some bending close, some weeping. Behind it stands Jesus, in light, holding a tiny figure wrapped in white, like a newborn. It's her soul. At the start of the Gospels, she carried him as a baby. In this picture, he carries her. The woman is Mary, the mother of Jesus. Orthodox Christians call this moment her falling asleep. Today's word: Dormition.
screen: `AN ICON: A WOMAN ON A BIER.`
`JESUS HOLDS HER SOUL LIKE A CHILD.`
`SHE CARRIED HIM. NOW HE CARRIES HER.`

segments.voice: In Luke, her answer to the angel ends in a yes: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." At the cross, in John, Jesus gives her into a disciple's care: "Behold thy mother! And from that hour that disciple took her unto his own home." The last time Acts names her, she is praying with the apostles: "Mary the mother of Jesus." After that, silence. The New Testament never tells how her life ended. So the churches keep this day in three ways. Orthodox Christians keep the Dormition, which means falling asleep. The New Testament can speak of the faithful dead as sleeping; of Stephen, stoned in Acts, the King James says simply, "he fell asleep." The Orthodox tradition holds that Mary truly died, surrounded by the apostles, that her Son received her soul, as the icon shows, and that her body too was then taken up to heaven. Catholics keep the fifteenth of August as the Assumption: Catholic teaching holds that at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken up, body and soul, into the glory of heaven. Protestants who don't hold either as a teaching give a plain reason: scripture doesn't tell the story. They honor her as Luke does, the faithful disciple who said yes all the way to the cross and the upper room, and some keep the day as a festival of Mary. What all three share is the woman in Luke who said, "all generations shall call me blessed," and a sense that the one who carried Jesus was not forgotten by him.

Think of a woman who carried someone, a mother, a grandmother, a neighbor who raised half the street, and of one thing she did again and again without applause: a packed lunch, a light left on. If you pray, thank God for her by name; if you don't, hold her with thanks. If she has died, you might picture her as the icon does, being carried now.
Dormition. The falling asleep of Mary, the Orthodox name for the end of her earthly life. Catholics keep the feast as the Assumption.
Your line: she fell asleep. In the icon, her Son carries her. Day one thousand forty-eight, done.

1049.title: Harvest festival
1049.hook: churches fill with produce, loaves and tins for food banks
1049.howItsDone: Churches and schools hold harvest festivals when the crops are in, decorating the church with produce and bread, singing harvest hymns, and collecting tins and packets for food banks or local charities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dormition: three ways the churches remember Mary. Your line was she fell asleep.

A marrow the size of a small dog lies across the front of the altar. Next to it, a basket of apples, a sheaf of wheat tied with string, a loaf baked in the shape of a wheatsheaf, and a pyramid of tinned tomatoes and baked beans leaning slightly to the left. A child walks up the aisle holding a single carrot as if it were a crown. The church smells of bread and earth. On Monday, the tins go in a van to the food bank. This is the harvest festival, and a harvest hymn sings that all good gifts around us are sent from heaven above.

Harvest festival isn't a single date in the church calendar. Churches, schools and villages hold it when the crops are in, often on a Sunday in the autumn. But the idea under it runs through the Bible. A psalm sings to God: "Thou crownest the year with thy goodness." The year has a crown, and the crown is food. The letter of James puts it plainly: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights." The hymn's line, all good gifts, echoes it. The food on the altar says: we didn't make this from nothing. Sun, rain, soil, seed, and a lot of other people's work came first. Then the second turn, just as old. The law of Moses tells farmers not to strip their fields bare. In the King James Bible: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." And if a farmer forgets a sheaf in the field, he's told not to go back for it: "it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow." The edges of the field belonged, by law, to the people with no field. That's why the tins matter: they're the corners of the field, in a supermarket age. So the harvest festival does two things at once. It looks up, in thanks. And it looks across, to the neighbor whose cupboard is empty.

Picture your own kitchen, the cupboard, the fridge, the shelf, and walk along it in your mind; pick one thing, a tin, a packet, a jar, that you could give away, something you'd be glad to eat yourself. If you pray, give thanks for the people whose work put it on your shelf; if you don't, just hold them in mind: the grower, the picker, the driver.
Harvest festival. A church's thanksgiving for the crops, when the altar fills with food, and much of the food goes to people who need it.
Your line: all good gifts. The corners of the field still belong to someone. See you tomorrow.

1050.title: Holy Cross Day (14 September)
1050.hook: the cross honored as a sign of victory, not only suffering
1050.howItsDone: On Holy Cross Day, Orthodox churches lift up a cross for the faithful to venerate, and Catholic and some Protestant churches read the scriptures of the cross; Christians in several traditions mark themselves with the sign of the cross in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harvest festival: tins on the altar, and the field's corners left for others. Your line was all good gifts.

"God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul wrote that to the churches in Galatia: a strange sentence. Glory, in a cross. In Paul's world, a cross was how Rome put people to death, and the letter to the Hebrews speaks of its shame. Not a thing to boast in. And yet people now trace it on their foreheads, raise it over altars, and hang it round their necks. One day in the church year honors the cross itself, not as a defeat but as a victory. Today, Holy Cross Day.

Good Friday looks at the cross with grief. Holy Cross Day looks at it with something closer to wonder. Orthodox Christians call it the Exaltation, or the Elevation, of the Cross: a cross is lifted high, and people bow before it. Catholics and some Protestant churches keep the day too. The story behind it is a tradition, not scripture: tradition says that Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine, searched in Jerusalem for the cross of Jesus, and that a church was built at the place. But the Bible gives the feast its turn of thought. In John, Jesus says, "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." Lifted up: execution and exaltation at once. Peter's first letter says Jesus "bare our sins in his own body on the tree." A tree. That word sends some readers back to the garden, where Genesis places "the tree of life also in the midst of the garden," and forward to Revelation, where the tree of life stands again by a river, and "the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations." Old hymns and sermons sing of the cross as a tree: dead wood become the tree of life. A tree in a garden at the start, a tree on a hill in the middle, a tree by a river at the end. That's why the day can be joyful. Christians don't forget the suffering. They honor the cross as the place where, they say, death lost.

segments.voice: If it's part of your practice, trace the cross slowly, forehead, chest, shoulder to shoulder, the way your church does; if not, simply bow your head, as people bow before the lifted cross. Then hold one thing in your life that feels like dead wood, and let a tree with healing leaves sit beside it.
Exaltation. The name Orthodox Christians give the feast that honors the cross as a sign of victory, the dead wood they call the tree of life.
Your line: the tree of life. It closes a week of feasts, from John's birth to the cross. Day one thousand fifty.
